subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement is one of the key assumptions of the ideal gas model?
items.correct: The particles have a negligible volume compared with the volume of the gas.
items.misconception: The particles lose a small amount of kinetic energy in every collision.
items.why: Everyday collisions (bouncing balls, snooker balls) always lose kinetic energy as heat and sound, and everyday experience says that moving things stop unless something keeps them going. Students apply this to particles without recognizing that the particles' motion is itself the thermal energy of the gas. Collisions between the particles of an ideal gas are elastic. At constant temperature the average kinetic energy of the particles stays constant indefinitely; the gas does not run down or settle.
items.specStatementText: An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
items.random_wrong: The spaces between the particles are filled with air that separates them.

items.q: According to the ideal gas model, what causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?
items.correct: Moving particles collide with the walls and exert a force on them.
items.misconception: The particles repel one another, so they push outwards on the walls.
items.why: A gas pushing out a piston or a balloon suggests that something inside is pushing outwards, so students picture particles pressing on their neighbours like compressed springs. A static 'repelling particles' picture was also an early historical model of gases, and it persists in students' explanations. The particles move freely between collisions. A gas spreads out because of this random motion, and its pressure comes from the collisions of the particles with the walls of the container.
items.specStatementText: An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
items.random_wrong: The weight of the particles presses on the container, mainly on its base.

items.q: A sample of nitrogen is held at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa, first at 150 K and then at 600 K. It is a gas at both temperatures. At which temperature does it deviate more from ideal gas behaviour, and why?
items.correct: At 150 K, as its slower particles are affected more by the attractions between them
items.misconception: At 150 K, as its particles have stopped moving and so no longer collide
items.why: Students link 'cold' with 'still', and school diagrams of solids show particles that look fixed in place. They generalize this to mean that low temperature brings motion to an end. As long as a substance is a gas, its particles move and collide; that is why it exerts a pressure. At low temperature they move more slowly, which is why the attractions between them become significant.
items.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
items.random_wrong: At 600 K, as its faster particles collide more violently with each other

items.q: Four gases are each at 300 K and 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Which gas deviates most from ideal gas behaviour?
items.correct: Ammonia, NH₃, as hydrogen bonding attracts its molecules to one another
items.misconception: Helium, He, as its light atoms move the fastest and collide most violently
items.why: Students associate energetic, 'extreme' conditions with things going wrong, and they connect the model's collisions with particle speed rather than with the balance between kinetic energy and intermolecular attraction. Deviation is greatest at low temperature and high pressure. Raising the temperature makes a real gas behave more ideally, because the particles' kinetic energy becomes large compared with the attractions between them.
items.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
items.random_wrong: Neon, Ne, as its atoms are the heaviest and so they occupy the most space

items.q: At STP (273 K, 100 kPa), 1.00 mol of helium (M = 4.00 g mol⁻¹) occupies 22.7 dm³. What volume does 1.00 mol of xenon (M = 131.29 g mol⁻¹) occupy at STP, if both behave as ideal gases?
items.correct: 22.7 dm³, as volume depends only on the amount of gas at a given T and p
items.misconception: 22.7 dm³, as heavy xenon atoms move at the same speed as the helium atoms
items.why:
Students learn that temperature is linked to the motion of particles and read 'motion' as 'speed', so equal temperatures seem to mean equal speeds. Kinetic energy, which depends on mass as well as speed, is less familiar than speed. Equal temperatures mean equal average kinetic energies, so heavier particles have lower average speeds. The molar volume is the same for all ideal gases because volume depends only on the number of particles, not because the particles move at the same speed.

Working: Both samples are at the same temperature (273 K) and pressure (100 kPa) and contain the same amount of gas (1.00 mol). For an ideal gas V = nRT/p, which does not contain the molar mass, so V(Xe) = V(He) = 1.00 mol × 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 22.7 dm³.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
items.random_wrong: More than 22.7 dm³, as its much larger atoms take up more of the space
items.working: Both samples are at the same temperature (273 K) and pressure (100 kPa) and contain the same amount of gas (1.00 mol). For an ideal gas V = nRT/p, which does not contain the molar mass, so V(Xe) = V(He) = 1.00 mol × 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 22.7 dm³.

items.q: What volume does 72.0 g of oxygen gas, O₂, occupy at STP (273 K, 100 kPa)? Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹; A_r(O) = 16.00.
items.why:
The periodic table gives one value per element and students write 'oxygen' as O. The diatomic formulas of hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and the halogens are learned as a list but not applied when a molar mass is needed. Use the formula of the substance actually present. Oxygen gas is O₂, so M(O₂) = 32.00 g mol⁻¹.

Working: M(O₂) = 2 × 16.00 = 32.00 g mol⁻¹. n(O₂) = m/M = 72.0 g ÷ 32.00 g mol⁻¹ = 2.25 mol. V = n × V_m = 2.25 mol × 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 51.1 dm³ = 5.11 × 10¹ dm³.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.

items.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas is kept at constant pressure. Its volume is measured at several temperatures and plotted against temperature in °C. Which description of the graph is correct?
items.correct: A straight line meeting the axis at −273 °C, where volume would be zero
items.misconception: A straight line meeting the axis at −273 °C, where the particles shrink to nothing
items.why: Students transfer the observable behaviour of the bulk gas (it expands, it fills its container) to its individual particles. Everyday talk of things 'expanding when heated', and diagrams that draw hotter gases with larger circles, reinforce it. It is one of the most widely reported misconceptions about the particle model. Particles keep the same size at every temperature. Heating increases their average kinetic energy, not their size. A heated gas occupies more space because faster particles collide with the walls harder and more often; the particles' own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
items.random_wrong: A straight line through the origin, since volume is proportional to temperature in °C

items.q: For a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature, the pressure, p, is plotted on the y-axis against 1/V on the x-axis, where V is the volume. Which description of the graph is correct?
items.correct: A straight line through the origin, as p doubles whenever V is halved
items.misconception: A straight line with a negative gradient, as p falls as 1/V rises
items.why: In everyday language 'inversely' just means 'the opposite way', and the decreasing graph students have drawn most often is a straight line sloping down. Confusing inverse proportion with a negative linear relationship is widely reported in mathematics and science education. Inverse proportion means that the product is constant: halving V doubles p. p against V is a curve; p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin with a positive gradient.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
items.random_wrong: A curve that falls and levels off, as p and V are inversely related

items.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas in a gas syringe is heated at constant pressure from 20 °C to 40 °C. What happens to its volume?
items.correct: It rises by about 7%, since its temperature in K does
items.misconception: It doubles, since 20 °C to 40 °C doubles its temperature
items.why: Celsius is the everyday temperature scale, and 'double one quantity, double the other' is applied to whatever numbers are given. In calculations students often simply forget to convert, because the equation looks the same whichever temperature is substituted. The gas relationships, PV = nRT and the combined gas law use absolute temperature: convert with T/K = t/°C + 273 before any calculation. On a Celsius axis the volume–temperature line meets the axis at −273 °C, not at 0 °C.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
items.random_wrong: It increases, since each gas particle expands when heated

items.q: What volume is occupied by 0.0472 mol of an ideal gas at 30 °C and 125 kPa? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
items.why:
Stems often quote pressures in kPa and volumes in cm³ or dm³. Students either substitute these directly or remember only that 'you divide by 1000', and apply that to cm³ as if it were dm³. The factor 10⁻⁶ for cm³ to m³ comes from cubing 10⁻² m, which is often not understood. Convert to SI before substituting: kPa × 10³ gives Pa; dm³ × 10⁻³ gives m³; cm³ × 10⁻⁶ gives m³ (1 cm = 10⁻² m, so 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³). PV is then in joules, matching R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

Working: T = 30 + 273 = 303 K; P = 125 kPa = 1.25 × 10⁵ Pa. V = nRT/P = (0.0472 mol × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ × 303 K) ÷ (1.25 × 10⁵ Pa) = 118.8 J ÷ (1.25 × 10⁵ Pa) = 9.51 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
items.specStatementText: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.

items.q: A gas syringe contains 2.20 cm³ of an ideal gas at 20 °C and 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa. What amount of gas does it contain? R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
items.why:
V = n × 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ is used so often that students remember the number but not the conditions attached to it, and 'the molar volume is a constant' is misremembered as 'the molar volume is one fixed number'. The molar volume is constant only at a specified temperature and pressure. 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ is its value at 273 K and 100 kPa; it is larger at higher temperature or lower pressure. At any other conditions use PV = nRT.

Working: T = 20 + 273 = 293 K; V = 2.20 cm³ = 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ m³. n = PV/RT = (1.20 × 10⁵ Pa × 2.20 × 10⁻⁶ m³) ÷ (8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ × 293 K) = 0.264 J ÷ 2435 J mol⁻¹ = 1.08 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
items.specStatementText: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.

items.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas occupies 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 27 °C. It is compressed to 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and at the same time its temperature rises to 87 °C. What is its new pressure?
items.why:
Students rearrange the symbols without checking the direction of the change, and ratios such as T₁/T₂ and T₂/T₁ look equally plausible on paper. After rearranging, check the direction of the change: heating at constant pressure must increase the volume; compressing at constant temperature must increase the pressure. V₂ = V₁ × T₂/T₁ and V = n × V_m.

Working: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T₂ = 87 + 273 = 360 K. From P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂: P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa × (2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ ÷ 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³) × (360 K ÷ 300 K) = 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa × 4.00 × 1.20 = 4.80 × 10⁵ Pa.
items.specStatementText: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.

items.q: A sample of methane, CH₄, is kept at 300 K, first at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and then at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. It is a gas at both pressures. At which pressure does it deviate more from ideal gas behaviour, and why?
items.correct: At 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, as its particles are close enough for their volume and attractions to matter
items.misconception: At 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, as its particles collide more often and lose kinetic energy each time
items.why: Everyday collisions (bouncing balls, snooker balls) always lose kinetic energy as heat and sound, and everyday experience says that moving things stop unless something keeps them going. Students apply this to particles without recognizing that the particles' motion is itself the thermal energy of the gas. Collisions between the particles of an ideal gas are elastic. At constant temperature the average kinetic energy of the particles stays constant indefinitely; the gas does not run down or settle.
items.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
items.random_wrong: At 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, as its particles expand to fill the much larger volume of the gas

items.q: The graph shows PV / nRT plotted against pressure for a real gas at constant temperature, together with the line for an ideal gas. Which statement explains the behaviour of the real gas at the point marked A?
items.correct: Attractions between the molecules pull them closer together, so the gas occupies a smaller volume than an ideal gas would.
items.misconception: The covalent bonds within each molecule are strong, and these bonds hold the neighbouring molecules close together.
items.why: The word 'bond' is used for both, and molecular diagrams show only the bonds inside a molecule. Confusing intramolecular bonds with intermolecular forces is one of the most widely reported misconceptions in chemistry education. How far a gas deviates from ideal behaviour depends on the intermolecular forces between its molecules, not on the covalent bonds within them. NH₃ molecules hydrogen bond to one another; CH₄ molecules attract one another only by London forces.
items.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
items.random_wrong: The molecules have a volume of their own, so the gas is squeezed into less space than the ideal model predicts.

items.q: The graph shows the volume of a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant pressure plotted against temperature in °C. Measurements were made between 27 °C and 227 °C and the line is extrapolated back to the temperature axis. At what temperature would the volume of the gas be 48.0 cm³?
items.why:
Students learn to convert to kelvin at the start of temperature calculations but treat the conversion as a one-way preliminary step, so the final kelvin value is reported with the unit the question used. Answers left in kelvin when °C was asked for are commonly noted in examiner reports. Check the unit asked for at the end of every calculation: 600 K is 600 − 273 = 327 °C.

Working: From the graph, V = 40.0 cm³ at 227 °C and the line extrapolates to V = 0 at −273 °C, so V ∝ T/K. T₁ = 227 + 273 = 500 K. T₂ = T₁ × V₂/V₁ = 500 K × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K; t₂ = 600 − 273 = 327 °C.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
items.working: From the graph, V = 40.0 cm³ at 227 °C and the line extrapolates to V = 0 at −273 °C, so V ∝ T/K. T₁ = 227 + 273 = 500 K. T₂ = T₁ × V₂/V₁ = 500 K × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K; t₂ = 600 − 273 = 327 °C.

items.q: Is the pressure of a gas caused by the weight of the gas?
items.correct: No. Gas pressure comes from the particles colliding with the walls, so it acts equally in all directions, including upwards on the lid of a container.
items.misconception: Gas pressure is caused by the weight of the gas pressing down, so it acts mainly downwards, on the base of the container.
items.why: Students first meet pressure for solids resting on surfaces and for liquids ('pressure increases with depth'), where weight is the cause, and carry the same explanation over to gases. Everyday talk of the air 'pressing down' on us reinforces it. The weight of the gas in a laboratory container is negligible. Its pressure is the force per unit area from particle collisions with every wall, so it is the same on the top, the sides and the base.
items.specStatementText: An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is in the space between the particles of a gas?
items.correct: Nothing: the space between the particles is empty. The particles' own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.
items.misconception: The spaces between gas particles are filled with air (or some other substance).
items.why: Empty space is hard to imagine, and students have long been told that 'air is everywhere'. Particle diagrams drawn on a coloured background look like a substance filling the gaps. Reluctance to accept empty space between particles is widely reported in research on students' particle ideas. Air is itself a mixture of gases made of particles, so it cannot fill the gaps between gas particles. In the ideal gas model the particles have negligible volume and the space between them is empty.
items.specStatementText: An ideal gas consists of moving particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular forces. All collisions between particles are considered elastic.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does one mole of a gas made of large, heavy particles occupy a larger volume than one mole of a gas made of small, light particles at the same temperature and pressure?
items.correct: No. The particles' own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the gas, so one mole of any ideal gas occupies the same volume at a given temperature and pressure.
items.misconception: Bigger or heavier particles take up more space, so the volume of a gas, and how much it deviates from ideal behaviour, depend on the size or mass of its particles.
items.why: In solids and liquids larger particles do take up more room, and students tend to equate a heavier particle with a larger one. They carry this over to gases without realizing that almost all of the volume of a gas is empty space. The volume of a gas is almost entirely the space between its particles, so at a given temperature and pressure it depends only on the number of particles. How far a gas deviates from ideal behaviour depends mainly on the strength of the attractions between its particles, not on their mass.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the mass of a gas be multiplied by the molar volume to find its volume?
items.correct: No. The molar volume is the volume per mole, so it must be multiplied by the amount in mol: first n = m/M, then V = n × V_m.
items.misconception: The mass of a substance can be used in place of its amount (in mol) in mole calculations.
items.why: Mass is the quantity measured on a balance and the one given in the question, and 'amount' in everyday speech means 'how much', which students take to mean mass. Convert mass to amount first, n = m/M, and only then multiply by the molar volume: V = n × V_m.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At the same temperature and pressure, are the particles of a less dense gas further apart?
items.correct: No. At the same temperature and pressure equal volumes of ideal gases contain equal numbers of particles, so the spacing is the same; a less dense gas has lighter particles.
items.misconception: A less dense gas has its particles further apart, so the same amount of it occupies a larger volume.
items.why: Density differences between solids and liquids are often explained by how closely the particles are packed, and students carry that explanation to gases compared at the same conditions, overlooking the mass of each particle. Density is mass divided by volume. At the same temperature and pressure the number of particles per unit volume is the same for all ideal gases, so differences in gas density come from the mass of each particle (the molar mass), not from spacing.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.

items.q: A gas is compressed and heated at the same time. Can its new pressure be found from the volume change alone?
items.correct: No. Both changes affect the pressure, so the combined gas law, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, including the temperature ratio, must be used.
items.misconception: Only the relationship between pressure and volume needs to be applied; a change in the third variable (temperature) can be ignored.
items.why: The pressure–volume, volume–temperature and pressure–temperature relationships are taught separately, each with the third variable held constant, and students carry the habit of 'one relationship at a time' into problems in which all three change. For a fixed mass of gas use the combined gas law, which includes every variable that changes. Simplify it only after checking which of P, V and T are genuinely constant.
items.specStatementText: The relationship between the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of an ideal gas is shown in the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the volume of a gas at constant pressure stay the same when it is heated, because a gas fills its container?
items.correct: No. At constant pressure (in a gas syringe, or behind a free piston) the gas expands when heated; its volume is proportional to its absolute temperature.
items.misconception: A gas always has the volume of its container, so heating it cannot change its volume.
items.why: Students learn that 'a gas has no fixed volume and fills its container' and picture every container as rigid. They do not recognize that keeping the pressure constant needs a container, such as a syringe, whose volume can change. A gas fills its container, but if the container can expand (constant pressure), heating increases the volume in proportion to the absolute temperature. Only in a rigid container is the volume fixed, and then the pressure rises instead.

items.q: Is a graph of p against 1/V a falling curve, like a graph of p against V?
items.correct: No. p against V is a falling curve; p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin, because p is directly proportional to 1/V.
items.misconception: The graph of an inverse relationship always looks like a falling curve, whatever is plotted on the x-axis.
items.why: Students remember graph shapes as pictures attached to a relationship ('inverse means a falling curve') and do not read the axis labels. Treating a graph as a picture rather than reading what is plotted is widely reported in research on graph interpretation. Read the axes before choosing a shape. Plotting p against 1/V turns the inverse relationship into a direct proportion, which gives a straight line through the origin.

items.q: Can the pressure of a gas change while its temperature stays constant?
items.correct: Yes. At constant temperature the average speed of the particles is unchanged, but compressing the gas makes them hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises.
items.misconception: Gas pressure depends only on how fast the particles move, so at constant temperature the pressure cannot change.
items.why: Students learn that heating a gas raises its pressure 'because the particles move faster' and make speed the only cause of pressure, forgetting how often the particles hit the walls. Pressure depends on how hard and how often the particles hit the walls. At constant temperature, reducing the volume increases the frequency of collisions with the walls, so p is inversely proportional to V.
items.specStatementText: The molar volume of an ideal gas is a constant at a specific temperature and pressure.

items.q: Why does PV/nRT for a real gas fall below 1 at moderate pressures?
items.correct: Because of the attractions between the particles: they pull the particles closer together, so the gas occupies a smaller volume (or exerts a lower pressure) than an ideal gas would. The particles’ own volume acts the other way, pushing PV/nRT above 1 at high pressure.
items.misconception: Every deviation from ideal behaviour, including PV/nRT falling below 1, is caused by the particles having a volume of their own.
items.why: ‘Particles have volume’ is the assumption students remember first, so it is offered as the reason for any deviation, without asking in which direction each limitation of the model pushes PV/nRT. Each limitation has its own direction. Attractions between particles reduce the volume or pressure, so PV/nRT < 1 (the dip at moderate pressure). The particles’ own volume makes the gas harder to compress, so PV/nRT > 1 at high pressure, where this effect dominates.
items.specStatementText: Real gases deviate from the ideal gas model, particularly at low temperature and high pressure.
